content.title: 10 CLI Tools Every Developer Should Know in 2026
content.text:
The command line is still the fastest way to get things done, and in 2026 there are more CLI tools than ever competing for a spot in your dotfiles. Whether you are a backend engineer, a frontend developer, or somewhere in between, the right terminal utilities can save you hours every week. In this post we round up 10 CLI tools every developer should know in 2026. Some are brand new, some are modern takes on classics, but all of them deserve a look.

1. Fennelgrep — A blazing fast search tool that respects your ignore files and highlights matches in colour. If you are still typing plain grep with a dozen flags, Fennelgrep will feel like a breath of fresh air. It is written in a compiled language, so searching a large monorepo takes seconds instead of minutes.

2. Larkfind — Think of Larkfind as find, but with sensible defaults. It skips hidden directories, understands glob patterns out of the box, and prints results you can actually read. Once you try it you will never go back to memorising the old syntax.

3. Quillcat — Quillcat is a drop-in replacement for cat that adds syntax highlighting, line numbers, and git change markers. It is perfect for quickly peeking at a file without opening an editor. It also pipes cleanly, so your scripts keep working.

4. Hopdir — Hopdir learns which directories you visit most and lets you jump to them with a few keystrokes. Say goodbye to typing long relative paths. After a day of use it will already know where you want to go.

5. Tallyproc — Tallyproc is a friendlier top. It shows CPU, memory, and network usage in a clean dashboard with colour-coded bars, and you can kill a runaway process directly from the interface. Great for those moments when your laptop fan spins up for no reason.

6. Sproutenv — Managing multiple language runtimes is painful, and Sproutenv makes it painless. Drop a version file in your project and the right toolchain is activated automatically when you cd in. It supports every major language and is easy to extend.

7. Pinehttp — Pinehttp is a human-friendly HTTP client for the terminal. Requests are short and readable, responses are pretty-printed, and sessions let you save auth headers between calls. It is the fastest way to poke at an API without opening a browser.

8. Ledgerdiff — Ledgerdiff makes diffs beautiful. It shows side-by-side changes with syntax highlighting and word-level markers, so you can see exactly what moved. Hook it into your version control tool and code reviews get easier instantly.

9. Reedjson — Reedjson slices and filters JSON from the command line. Pipe any API response into it and pull out exactly the fields you need with a compact query language. Every developer who works with APIs should have this installed.

10. Moorshell — Moorshell is a modern shell with autosuggestions, syntax highlighting, and sane scripting. It works well out of the box with no configuration, which makes it a great choice if you want a nicer terminal without spending a weekend on setup.

There you have it: 10 CLI tools every developer should know in 2026. Each one solves a small annoyance, and together they add up to a much smoother workflow. Try installing a couple this week and see how quickly they become habits. Did we miss your favourite? Let us know in the comments which tools you cannot live without, and share this list with a teammate who is still using the defaults.
